articles.title: Reform Judaism in Plain Words
articles.summary: What Reform Jews hold on to, what they leave to personal choice, and how the movement has written down its beliefs over time.

terms.en: teaching; the Five Books of Moses

sections.heading: Three Words at the Centre
paras: Reform Judaism keeps three old ideas at its centre: God, Torah and Israel. Israel here means the Jewish people, not only the country. Around that centre, Reform Jews believe and practise in many different ways, and the movement says so openly.
In North America the movement is led by the Union for Reform Judaism. Its rabbis belong to the Central Conference of American Rabbis, and that body has written the movement's statements of belief.

sections.heading: Beliefs Written Down, Then Rewritten
paras: Reform rabbis have put their beliefs on paper several times. The first was the Pittsburgh Platform of 1885. Later statements came in 1937 in Columbus, in 1976 in San Francisco and in 1999, again in Pittsburgh.

Each one reads differently, and that is the point. The 1885 text set aside much of traditional ritual. The 1999 statement invited Reform Jews to look again at traditional practice and choose what gives their lives holiness. You can read every one of these documents on the rabbis' own website.

sections.heading: Choice, Learning and Welcome
paras: A Reform Jew is asked to learn first, then make thoughtful choices about how to live out Jewish values, weighing each mitzvah on its merits. The movement says plainly that there is more than one real way to be Jewish.

The movement also puts a lot of weight on repairing the world, which it calls tikkun olam. And it works to welcome everyone: in 2015 it affirmed full inclusion of people of all gender identities and gender expressions.

articles.title: Shabbat at Home
articles.summary: Candles, wine, two loaves and a blessing for the children: the Friday night table, step by step, and why each piece is there.

terms.en: the blessing that makes the day holy, said over wine
the short ceremony that ends Shabbat

sections.heading: From Sundown to Stars
paras: Shabbat starts at sundown on Friday. It ends on Saturday evening with Havdalah, a few minutes of blessings over wine, spices and a braided candle that mark the line between the holy day and the week.
People greet each other with Shabbat shalom, a wish for a peaceful Sabbath.

sections.heading: Two Candles
paras: Most homes light at least two candles. The Torah tells us about Shabbat twice, once to remember it (Exodus 20:8) and once to keep it (Deuteronomy 5:12), and each candle stands for one of those verses.
Here's a detail that surprises people: the candles are lit first and the blessing comes after. Saying the blessing is what begins Shabbat, so you light while it is still a weekday.

sections.heading: Wine, Bread and Children
paras: Kiddush comes next, said over wine. Grape juice works just as well for children or anyone who doesn't drink.

Then two whole loaves of challah. They recall the double portion of manna that fell in the desert before each Sabbath, so no one had to gather food on the day of rest (Exodus 16). Many families also bless their children at the table, using words from Genesis 48:20.
After that, eat slowly. The meal itself is part of the day.

articles.title: How the Jewish Calendar Works
articles.summary: Months that follow the moon, years that follow the sun, and the extra month that keeps Passover in spring.

terms.en: month; from the word for new
the first day of a Hebrew month
a leap year; literally a pregnant year

sections.heading: Moon Months
paras: A Hebrew month, a chodesh, runs from one new moon to the next, so it lasts 29 or 30 days. Its first day is called Rosh Chodesh, the head of the month. Twelve of those months add up to about 354 days.

The sun's year is longer, roughly 365 and a quarter days. Left alone, a calendar of moon months would slip about 11 days earlier every year, and the spring festival of Passover would wander into winter, then autumn.

sections.heading: The Thirteenth Month
paras: The fix is to add a whole month now and then. Seven times in every 19 years, the year gets a second month of Adar. The two are called Adar I and Adar II, and Hebrew calls that kind of year shanah me'uberet, a pregnant year.
Tradition credits a sage named Hillel II with fixing this 19-year cycle in advance, and the same system is still used. In those years Purim, normally on the 14th of Adar, is kept in Adar II.

sections.heading: Days Start at Dusk
paras: A Jewish day begins at sunset, not midnight. That's why Shabbat and every festival start in the evening, and why the calendar in ALEF marks the evening before each holy day.

articles.title: Rosh HaShanah and Yom Kippur
articles.summary: Ten days that start with a new year and end with a fast: what teshuvah means and what you'll hear and see in the synagogue.

terms.en: the new year; literally head of the year
a ram's horn blown like a trumpet

sections.heading: Ten Days of Awe
paras: Rosh HaShanah, the Jewish new year, falls on the first of Tishrei. It opens ten days called the Days of Awe, and those days close with Yom Kippur on the tenth.

The theme of the whole stretch is teshuvah. The word means turning, and the idea is practical: notice where you went wrong, make it right with the people involved, and come back to the person you want to be.

sections.heading: The Sound of the Shofar
paras: A shofar is a ram's horn, and its raw sound is the signature of the season. It is blown during the month of Elul as a reminder that the holy days are coming, on Rosh HaShanah itself, and one last time when Yom Kippur ends.
On the first day, often in the afternoon, many people go to a river or other moving water for Tashlich. They toss in bits of bread as a picture of casting away the year's wrongs.

sections.heading: A Day Without Food
paras: Yom Kippur is the most solemn day of the year. Many adults fast from evening to evening and spend much of the day in prayer. More people come to synagogue on these days than at any other time.
Most Reform congregations keep one day of Rosh HaShanah, though a growing number now keep two.

articles.title: Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret and Simchat Torah
articles.summary: A week in a hut with a leafy roof, a bundle of branches and a citron, and a party for the Torah at the end.

terms.en: a temporary hut with a leafy roof
palm branch, bound with myrtle and willow

sections.heading: Living Outside
paras: Five days after Yom Kippur comes Sukkot, a harvest festival. It also recalls the forty years the Israelites spent in the desert after leaving Egypt, living in shelters that could be taken down and moved.
So people build a sukkah, a hut with a roof of branches, and eat their meals in it for the week. The Torah's own instruction is short: live in booths for seven days (Leviticus 23:42).

sections.heading: Four Plants
paras: Sukkot's other symbol is held in two hands. The lulav is a palm branch bound with myrtle and willow; the etrog is a citron. After a blessing they are waved in six directions: east, south, west, north, up and down.

sections.heading: Dancing With the Scrolls
paras: On the eighth day comes Shemini Atzeret. Reform congregations and Jews in Israel celebrate Simchat Torah on that same day. The last lines of Deuteronomy are read, then the first lines of Genesis straight after, so the reading never really stops. People sing and dance with the Torah scrolls.

articles.title: Hanukkah, Then and Now
articles.summary: A rededicated Temple, a later story about oil, and eight nights of lights in the window.

terms.en: the helper candle that lights the others

sections.heading: What Happened
paras: Hanukkah means dedication. In the second century before the common era, a Jewish rebel group led by the Maccabees won Jerusalem back from its Syrian-Greek rulers and rededicated the Temple. They celebrated for eight days, matching the eight days of Sukkot.
Hanukkah isn't in the Torah. The sages added it later, and it begins on the 25th of Kislev.

sections.heading: The Oil
paras: The famous story of a small jar of oil that burned for eight days doesn't appear in the books of the Maccabees. It shows up centuries later, in the Talmud. Both stories are part of the holiday now, and many families tell them side by side.

sections.heading: Lighting the Lamp
paras: The hanukkiyah has nine branches: eight for the nights and one, the shamash, that lights the rest. You light one candle the first night and add one each night until all eight are burning. The lamp goes in a window or by the door so people passing can see it.
Foods fried in oil, like latkes and doughnuts, belong to the same story.

articles.title: Purim and the Book of Esther
articles.summary: A noisy reading of a scroll, food for friends and money for people in need: the four things Purim asks of you.

terms.en: scroll; here, the Book of Esther

sections.heading: The Story
paras: The Book of Esther tells of a Persian court where an official named Haman plots to destroy the Jews. Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai turn the plot around. Purim falls on the 14th of Adar, and in a leap year it moves to Adar II.
The book is read aloud from a scroll called the megillah, and the room makes as much noise as it can every time Haman's name comes up.

sections.heading: Four Things to Do
paras: Four duties belong to the day, as the rabbis listed them: hear the megillah, send food to friends, give to people in need, and sit down to a festive meal.
Mishloach manot, the food gift, has a simple rule: at least two kinds of ready-to-eat food, to at least one person. Three-cornered cookies called hamantaschen are a favourite.
Matanot la'evyonim, the gifts to the poor, exist so that everyone can afford to celebrate. Many Reform families give to a food bank or volunteer at a meal program that week.

articles.title: Pesach and the Seder
articles.summary: A meal in a set order that walks you from slavery to freedom, with a plate of symbols in the middle of the table.

terms.en: the telling; the book used at the seder

sections.heading: A Meal With an Order
paras: Pesach remembers the Exodus, the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt. Its heart is the seder, a festive home meal. Seder means order, because the evening follows a fixed sequence of about fifteen steps, from blessing the wine to songs at the end.
The steps are written out in a book called the Haggadah, which means the telling. Many versions exist, from traditional to playful, and many congregations also hold a community seder.

sections.heading: The Seder Plate
paras: A special plate sits near whoever leads. On it you'll usually find a roasted shank bone, an egg, a green vegetable such as parsley, a bitter herb, lettuce, and charoset, a sweet mix of fruit and nuts. Each one is pointed to and explained during the evening.
The greens are dipped in salt water, a taste of tears. A bitter herb stands for the bitterness of slavery, and charoset looks like the mortar the slaves used for bricks.

sections.heading: A Week Without Bread
paras: For the whole festival, leavened food, called chametz, is cleared out of the home and matzah takes the place of bread.

articles.title: Shavuot: Seven Weeks Later
articles.summary: A harvest festival that became the day of the giving of the Torah, with the Book of Ruth, dairy food and confirmation.

terms.en: the Book of Ruth, read on Shavuot

sections.heading: Counting From Passover
paras: Shavuot means weeks. It comes seven weeks after Pesach, which links leaving Egypt with arriving at Mount Sinai.

It began as a harvest festival, when the first fruits were brought to the Temple. The link to matan Torah, the giving of the Torah, came later, after the Temple was destroyed. The Torah itself doesn't make that connection.

sections.heading: Ruth, Cheesecake and Confirmation
paras: Many synagogues read the Book of Ruth. Ruth chose to join the Jewish people, and one reason given for reading her story now is that, like the Israelites at Sinai, she took on the covenant herself.
Dairy food is traditional, cheesecake and blintzes especially. People connect it with the sweetness of Torah and with the land the Torah calls flowing with milk and honey (Exodus 3:8).
Reform congregations often hold confirmation on or near Shavuot, for teenagers who kept studying after their bar or bat mitzvah.

articles.title: How a Service Flows
articles.summary: Open a prayer book and it can look endless. It isn't: a service has a few big blocks, always in the same order.

terms.en: prayer book; from the word for order
hear; the line that declares God is one

sections.heading: Warming Up
paras: Open a siddur, a prayer book, at the morning service and you'll find it begins with short blessings of thanks for ordinary things and a set of psalms. These were first said at home while getting up and dressing. They help you arrive before the main prayers start.

sections.heading: The Shema and Its Blessings
paras: Then the leader calls the room to prayer with Barchu, and the congregation answers. Two blessings follow, one about creation and one about the gift of Torah. Then comes the Shema itself: Hear, O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One (Deuteronomy 6:4). One more blessing after it gives thanks for freedom from Egypt.
The Shema is said morning and evening. It isn't a request at all. It's a statement that God is one.

sections.heading: Standing Prayer
paras: Next is the Amidah, which means standing, because you say it on your feet. It opens with praise and closes with thanks. On weekdays the middle holds requests; on Shabbat those are left out and the middle is about the day itself.
Many people say it quietly, at their own pace. Saying it in English is fine, and so is adding words of your own.

sections.heading: Torah and the Ending
paras: On Shabbat morning, and briefly on Mondays and Thursdays, a Torah scroll is taken out and read. The service then winds down with Aleinu, the Mourner's Kaddish and a closing song such as Adon Olam.

articles.title: The Torah, a Week at a Time
articles.summary: Why every Shabbat has a named reading, how the year's cycle starts again, and who gets called up.

terms.en: a reading from the Prophets after the Torah
going up; being called to bless the reading

sections.heading: Fifty-Four Portions
paras: The Torah, the Five Books of Moses, is split into 54 portions. Each one is a parashah. Each one takes its name from its first distinctive word or words. The first portion is Bereishit, which means in the beginning.
One portion is chanted from the scroll each Shabbat morning. A regular year has fewer Shabbatot than portions, so a few short ones are read in pairs to finish on time.

sections.heading: Round and Round
paras: The cycle ends and starts again on Simchat Torah. The last verses of Deuteronomy are read and the first of Genesis follow right away, so the scroll never sits finished.
After the Torah comes the haftarah, a reading from the Prophets picked to echo the week's portion.

sections.heading: Being Called Up
paras: The reading is divided into sections, and members of the congregation are invited up to say a blessing before and after each one. That honour is called an aliyah, which means going up.

articles.title: How Hebrew Came Back
articles.summary: For centuries Hebrew was for prayer and study. Then one stubborn family started speaking it at breakfast.

sections.heading: A Language Kept for Study
paras: Hebrew, Ivrit, never disappeared. Jews prayed in it, studied in it and wrote letters about religious questions in it. What it had lost, for many centuries, was everyday speech: nobody grew up talking about breakfast or the weather in Hebrew.

sections.heading: One Household
paras: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, born in 1858 in the village of Luzhky, set out to change that. He reached Jerusalem in 1881 and, with his wife Deborah, made their home a Hebrew-only home. Their son Ben-Zion became the first child in modern times raised with Hebrew as his mother tongue.
The thinking was simple. If a child could grow up speaking Hebrew, a whole people could.

sections.heading: Schools, Newspapers and New Words
paras: Ben-Yehuda pushed for Hebrew as the language of teaching in schools, which turned out to matter most. He ran newspapers, invented words for modern things and began a huge dictionary in 1910 that took seventeen volumes and was finished long after his death in 1922.
He also helped found the Hebrew Language Committee, Va'ad HaLashon, which grew into today's Academy of the Hebrew Language. When you learn a word like milon in ALEF, you're using his work.
